Solution 3 is the only one with the correct answer, 2/17.

**Solution 3's recursion.** Let P(n) be the probability that Michael and James are ever in the same group when n players remain, with n ≡ 1 (mod 3). There are three cases in the next round:
- Both are chosen, with probability 12/(n(n−1)). They meet.
- Exactly one is chosen, with probability 8(n−4)/(n(n−1)). They both stay in the game only if the chosen one wins, which has probability 1/4. Then n−3 players remain, including both of them.
- Neither is chosen, with probability (n−4)(n−5)/(n(n−1)). Both stay, with n−3 players remaining.

Combining the last two cases gives P(n) = 12/(n(n−1)) + [(n−4)(n−3)/(n(n−1))]·P(n−3).

**Closed form.** The base case is P(4) = 1. Substituting P(n−3) = 4/(n−3) into the right side gives (12 + 4(n−4))/(n(n−1)) = 4(n−1)/(n(n−1)) = 4/n. So P(n) = 4/n for all n ≡ 1 (mod 3), and P(34) = 4/34 = 2/17.

**Cross-check.** Solution 2's hand enumeration gives 4/7 for n = 7 and 2/5 for n = 10, which agree with 4/n.

**Why the others fail.**
- Solution 1 treats "exactly one chosen" as a case where they can never meet again. That is wrong, because the chosen one can win and both then stay in the game. It also never reached a final answer; its output ends at an unfinished factorization.
- Solution 2 guesses 2/g ≈ 1/2 from an approximation. Its own small cases contradict that value.

CHOICE: 3
